title.en: Exploring Substances: Acidic, Basic and Neutral

text.en: Lemon juice tastes sour. Soap feels slippery. Both are chemical substances, but they behave in opposite ways. We can test them with natural colour changers called indicators.

Acids taste sour, like lemon, tamarind and vinegar. Bases taste bitter and feel soapy, like baking soda and soap. Never taste unknown substances in the lab. We use indicators instead.
An indicator changes colour in acids and bases. Litmus paper turns from blue to red in acid and from red to blue in base. Turmeric turns red in bases. Red cabbage juice and China rose also change colour. A neutral substance, like pure water, does not change the colour of litmus.
Acids are used in food and in cleaning. Bases are used in soaps and antacids. Neutralisation is the reaction when an acid and a base cancel each other's effect to form salt and water. An antacid tablet neutralises extra acid in the stomach. Ant bite contains formic acid, and rubbing a base like baking soda soothes it.

problem.en: Blue litmus turns red in a solution. What is it?

text.en: Blue litmus turns red in acid.

prompt.en: Explain why we should not taste substances to find out if they are acidic.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all sour things are the same strength.

points.en: Acids are sour; bases are bitter and soapy.
Litmus: acid turns blue to red; base turns red to blue.
